intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair-1 (NSLH1) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene (602775) on chromosome 10q25.2.

paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair is characterized by Noonan-like facial features, including macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears. Patients also have a short webbed neck and pectus anomalies. Other features include reduced growth, often with proven growth hormone (GH) deficiency, cognitive deficits, and hyperactive behavior that improves with age. The hair is easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing, and is loose anagen hair on microscopy. Most patients have darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis, cardiac anomalies are common, and the voice is hypernasal (Cordeddu et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1991) reported a 4.5-year-old girl with Noonan syndrome and loose anagen hair. Her hair was short and blond, had never been cut, and was easily plucked. Scalp biopsy showed marked cleft formation between fragmented inner root sheaths and irregularly shaped hair shafts.

paragraphs.text: Tosti et al. (1997) reported 19 patients who had been diagnosed with loose anagen hair (LAH) at a university medical center since 1990. There were 14 children and 5 adults, aged 8 months to 47 years. Associated diseases included Noonan syndrome in a 5-year-old boy and alopecia areata in a 3-year-old boy. In all cases, the trichogram showed mostly anagen hairs (80 to 100%) without sheaths. LAH could begin in adulthood: 3 sporadic adults had diffuse hair shedding that started suddenly 1 to 3 years before evaluation. The authors noted that adult-onset LAH can easily be misdiagnosed as telogen hair loss. On follow-up, LAH remained stable in 4 children and 1 adult, and hair density improved considerably in 2 children and 1 adult.

They also had a short neck with redundant skin, severe GH deficiency, and mild psychomotor delay with attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). All 3 had an unusual combination of ectodermal abnormalities, including darkly pigmented hairless skin and hair defined as loose anagen hair.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that 25 individuals with the SHOC2 S2G mutation shared a consistent phenotype. Facial features were Noonan-like, with macrocephaly, high forehead, hypertelorism, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears. Patients also had a short webbed neck and pectus anomalies. Growth was reduced, frequently with proven GH deficiency. They had cognitive deficits and hyperactive behavior that improved with age. The hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing, and loose anagen hair was confirmed microscopically in 12 patients. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Cardiac anomalies were common, with mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects overrepresented, and the voice was hypernasal. In infancy, several patients had been thought to resemble Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Hoban et al. (2012) reported a male infant with a SHOC2 mutation who was delivered prematurely at 32 weeks because of fetal distress. After birth he had dysmorphic features, edema, hepatosplenomegaly, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and respiratory distress. Echocardiogram showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The cardiac lesion progressed quickly, and he was discharged home for palliative care. The authors stated that his cardiac findings and other features were not typical of previously reported individuals with this mutation and expanded the clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Gripp et al. (2013) reported 5 unrelated male patients with Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair who carried the SHOC2 p.Ser2Gly mutation. All 5 had skin hyperpigmentation, sparse light-colored hair, increased fine wrinkles, ligamentous laxity, developmental delay, and unusually long eyelashes (dolichocilia). All 4 patients who were assessed had a structural cardiac anomaly. Hypotonia and macrocephaly were each present in 4 of 5 patients. Polyhydramnios, increased birth weight, and use of a feeding tube were each present in 3 of 5. The authors described distinctive brain abnormalities: relative megalencephaly with enlarged subarachnoid spaces suggestive of benign external hydrocephalus, and a relatively small posterior fossa indicated by a vertical tentorium (4 of 4). They suggested that this combination accounted for the high rate of cerebellar tonsillar ectopia (3 of 4). Including cases from the literature, 3 of 8 patients who had MRI showed a Chiari I malformation.

paragraphs.text: Patient 1 of Gripp et al. (2013) was a boy born to 37-year-old parents after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios and cystic hygroma. He was macrosomic at birth. He had pyloric stenosis, severe failure to thrive needing a gastrostomy tube, mild pulmonic valve stenosis, low axial tone, small optic nerves, motor delay, and an OFC of +3 SD. Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia was suspected at age 2 years 3 months. He developed hepatosplenomegaly, and bone marrow biopsy was most consistent with primary myelofibrosis. The karyotype was normal, and there was no monosomy 7 and no JAK2 p.Val617Phe mutation. He died at age 2.5 years after a splenectomy performed in preparation for bone marrow transplant. This was the first hematologic neoplasm reported in a patient with a SHOC2 mutation.

paragraphs.text: Patient 4 of Gripp et al. (2013) was a boy of Mexican ancestry with global developmental delay and mild to moderate intellectual disability. He had an atrial septal defect, blond, sparse, easily pluckable hair, and long eyelashes. Brain MRI showed mild ventriculomegaly, periventricular nodular heterotopia, and a thick, dysplastic corpus callosum. By age 6 years he had developed a Chiari I malformation with platybasia and basilar invagination, together with C3-C4 vertebral fusion and unusual venous sinus anatomy. paragraphs.text: Young et al. (2018) showed that MRAS interacts with SHOC2 and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to form a heterotrimeric holoenzyme. This complex dephosphorylates the inhibitory S259 site on RAF kinases (S259 on CRAF, S365 on BRAF). MRAS and SHOC2 acted as PP1 regulatory subunits that make the complex highly specific for RAF. MRAS also acted as a targeting subunit, because the complex needed membrane localization to dephosphorylate RAF efficiently and to regulate the ERK pathway in cells. The predicted structure of SHOC2 closely resembles the A subunit of PP2A. The authors identified several regions in SHOC2 involved in complex formation, as well as residues in MRAS that help explain why MRAS binds specifically to SHOC2-PP1. Noonan syndrome mutations in SHOC2, MRAS, and PPP1CB always promoted formation of the complex with the other 2 partners, but did not necessarily promote binding to other interactors. The authors concluded that, at the biochemical level, Noonan syndrome in people with SHOC2, MRAS, or PPP1CB mutations is likely driven by enhanced formation of the ternary complex.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) sequenced SHOC2 in 96 patients with Noonan syndrome who did not have mutations in known genes. In 4 unrelated sporadic individuals, they identified a heterozygous 4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. The mutation was absent from the parents in the 3 families tested and was present in several tissues. In a further 410 mutation-negative subjects with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype, they found the mutation in 21 patients. It occurred de novo in all 12 families with available parental DNA. The substitution created an N-myristoylation site: the mutant protein incorporated [3H]-myristic acid in Cos-1 cells. It was constitutively targeted to the plasma membrane in a myristoylation-dependent manner and failed to translocate to the nucleus upon EGF stimulation. It enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation in Neuro2A cells.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-year-old girl of European ancestry with a RASopathy phenotype and in her father, Hannig et al. (2014) identified a heterozygous c.519G-A variant in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a met173-to-ile (M173I) substitution. The variant was found by sequencing a RASopathy gene panel, and the proband had inherited it from her father. The variant was not found in 6,500 asymptomatic individuals, and Met173 is conserved among vertebrate SHOC2 orthologs. The girl had macrocephaly, ptosis, and sparse, slow-growing hair. She did not have short stature, a cardiac anomaly, hyperpigmentation, or loose anagen hair. In SHOC2-depleted Cos1 cells, the mutant restored EGF-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation by only about 10% above basal levels. It also failed to precipitate PP1c effectively. The authors concluded that p.M173I causes loss of function in the ERK1/2 pathway.
